svg.title: Landing distance: speed, brakes and the runway you really have
svg.desc: PHAK story drawn to scale on a 3,500 foot runway: already 1,000 feet down the runway at 50 feet AGL, planned landing 1,600 feet, 320 feet more for 10 percent excess speed and 320 feet more for a 10 knot tailwind, leaving 260 feet spare before hydroplaning with locked brakes. Excess landing speed adds at least 21 percent to the distance and loads the brakes; aerodynamic drag helps down to 60 to 70 percent of touchdown speed. Landing charts use landing weight, not takeoff weight.
svg.text: Landing distance: speed, brakes and the runway you really have
Landing distance is predicted from the AFM/POH data and compared with the available runway. The bar
below uses the PHAK example of a high, fast, tailwind approach to a 3,500-foot runway, drawn to scale.
1,000 ft already used
at 50 ft AGL
Planned: 1,600 ft
10% too fast
10 kt tailwind
Runway 3,500 ft (to scale)
The pilot is at 70 knots planned but 80 knots actual
(10 percent high): +20 percent, 1,600 to 1,920 ft.
The 10-knot tailwind adds another 320 ft: 2,240 ft
after 50 ft AGL. Total needed 3,240 ft.
Hard braking then locks the wheels: the airplane
hydroplanes on the wet runway down to about 54 knots
(9 times the square root of the tire pressure, 36) and
braking is ineffective. The 300 to 500 ft lost takes
the 260 ft spare.
Why too much speed costs distance
A 10 percent excess landing speed causes at least
a 21 percent increase in landing distance (the
story above uses 20 percent)
More kinetic energy to dissipate: a greater
working load on the brakes
More lift in the ground attitude: less force on
the braking surfaces, a blown tire is more
probable
Landing below the AFM/POH speed risks a stall,
poor control or a high descent rate
Slowing down, and the worst case
Aerodynamic drag works down to 60 or 70 percent
of touchdown speed; below that brakes do the work
Keep thrust at the smallest possible positive
value during the roll
Most critical: high gross weight, high density
altitude and unfavorable wind together
Landing accounts for more pilot-caused accidents
than any other phase
Reading landing charts: use the landing weight, not the takeoff weight. Fuel burned must be taken off
Table (Figure 11-32): 1,250 ft is halfway between sea level (1,075 ft) and 2,500 ft (1,135 ft), so average
them: 1,105 ft over a 50-ft obstacle; ground roll 457.5 ft
Graph (Figure 11-33): 57 °F, 4,000 ft, 2,400 lb, 6 kt headwind, 50-ft obstacle: ground roll 975 ft, total
